summary: A 1979 note on how to address mail to hosts that are outside the network, including the form of such out-of-net addresses. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 754 compares four ways to address mail for people outside the ARPANET. It recommends a structured mailbox name that identifies both the destination network and user.

questions: out of net host addresses for mail
how to address mail to other networks
how did rfc 754 address mail outside the arpanet
subtitle: Four short-term ways to address mail to users outside the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET mail system needed a way to route messages to users on other networks while older and newer message systems operated together.
tldr.mechanism: The memo compares four schemes using forwarding mailboxes, message headers, per-user mailboxes, or structured names combining network and user.
tldr.outcome: The author recommends structured names because the FTP server at the forwarding host can route by a shared network prefix.

today: RFC 754 is a discussion of short-term approaches to mail addressing for hosts outside the ARPANET. It recommends Solution D, structured names.

sections.title: Mail to Other Networks
sections.content:
The memo considers how ARPANET mail could reach users on other networks during a transition to a broader Internet environment. It lists goals including limiting changes to existing software, gaining user acceptance, and limiting special transition software.

The four alternatives differ in where the forwarding host obtains the destination information: from new message headers, existing headers, per-user mailbox names, or a structured mailbox name.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages need an address that a forwarding host can use to deliver mail outside the ARPANET. The memo compares alternatives and their effects on programs and users.

sections.title: Four Addressing Alternatives
sections.content:
Solution A sends all external mail to one mailbox and adds new header lines with the external recipient. Solution B also uses one mailbox, but uses existing header lines. Solution C assigns per-user mailboxes at the forwarding host and relies on message headers to identify the destination.

Solution D uses a distinct mailbox name with a common network part and a unique user part, such as NSW-Joe. The FTP server recognizes the common prefix and retains the mailbox argument for the routing daemon.
sections.plainLanguage: The first three methods use headers or mailbox records in different ways. The fourth puts the network name and user name together in the mailbox identifier.

sections.title: Why Structured Names Are Recommended
sections.content:
The comparison says Solution D requires a change to the FTP server at the forwarding host, while no changes are needed to mail composition or processing programs. The routing daemon can use the mailbox argument without parsing message headers.

The memo recommends Solution D and notes that the syntax shown is only an example; other forms combining network and user could also work.
sections.plainLanguage: The author favors structured names because the forwarding server can recognize a network prefix without changing mail composition and reading programs.
